newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Pope warns of hedonism flowing to East Europe.
newsitem.headline: Pope warns of hedonism flowing to East Europe.

text.p: Pope John Paul began a visit to the Czech Republic on Friday praising Eastern Europe's post-communist rebirth but warning that hedonism was flowing in from the West.

The 76-year-old Polish Pontiff, who has suffered from a series of ailments in recent years, looked healthy and jovial as he flew in to mark the 1,000th anniversary of the martyrdom St Adalbert, who brought Christianity to Bohemia.

Asked by reporters whether he was disillusioned by social changes in eastern Europe since the fall of communist in 1989, he said: "I'm rather content, but without any illusions. One could foresee that after so many years not everything could be perfect."

The Pontiff, who influenced events that led to the fall of the Berlin Wall, was greeted at the airport by Czech President Vaclav Havel, a former dissident playwright who was imprisoned under the communists.
Havel said in a speech at the airport that St Adalbert had cherished a dream of European spiritual unity and saw his Czech homeland as part of the Christian community of the continent.
"This community was to be based on a spiritual and moral renewal and on readiness to embrace common values -- which is needed today just as it was then," Havel said.
In his arrival address, the Pope praised Havel as being "among those who brought about the rebirth of this country".

In a speech to Czech bishops in the Vatican embassy here, the Pope returned to his concern for moral values in the Czech Republic, which has one of the highest standards of living in eastern Europe and a highly secularised society.
The Pope lashed out at "hedonism, which has invaded these lands from neighbouring countries, and contributed to a growing crisis of values in everyday life".
He also spoke of the dangers to Czech society from "the infiltration of certain ideas already widespread in the West".

In his speech to the bishops he denounced the country's high abortion rate and said that the spread of pornography, prostitution and paedophilia were "symptomatic of a situation of grave social malaise".
Czech society, the Pope said, was still paying a heavy price for 40 years of systematic repression of the church.
Church-state relations in the former Czechoslovakia, which split peacefully into the Czech and Slovak Republics in 1993, were among the worst among the former East Bloc.

The Pope, making his third trip to Prague and his 76th abroad, paid tribute to late Cardinal Frantisek Tomasek, one of the towering anti-communist churchmen in eastern Europe during the Cold War years, and who died in 1992, aged 93, after living to see his dream of a free Czechoslovakia.
The Pope also told the bishops they should seek full restitution of church properties confiscated under Communism.
The government has returned a number of churches and properties since the fall of communism but the status of many others is still unresolved.

The Pope is due to celebrate a mass on Saturday morning with young people in the town of Hradec Kralove, some 100 km (60 miles) east of the capital, to mark the anniversary of the martyrdom St Adalbert who brought Christianity to Bohemia.
The saint, Vojtech in Czech, was the first bishop of Czech origin, but also took Christian faith to the Pope's native Poland and is seen by Catholics as "an apostle of Europe".
The Pope, 77 on May 18, is also due to celebrate an outdoor mass in Prague on Sunday, and preside at an ecumenical service in the capital's St Vitus cathedral before returning to Rome.
